title: Biological Correlates of Extinction Risk in Bats
abstract: We investigated patterns and processes of extinction and threat in bats using a multivariate phylogenetic comparative approach. Of nearly 1,000 species worldwide, 239 are considered threatened by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) and 12 are extinct. Small geographic ranges and low wing aspect ratios are independently found to predict extinction risk in bats, which explains 48% of the total variance in IUCN assessments of threat. The pattern and correlates of extinction risk in the two bat suborders are signiﬁcantly different. A higher proportion (4%) of megachiropteran species have gone extinct in the last 500 years than microchiropteran bats (0.3%), and a higher proportion is currently at risk of extinction (Megachiroptera: 34%; Microchiroptera: 22%). While correlates of microchiropteran extinction risk are the same as in the order as a whole, megachiropteran extinction is correlated more with reproductive rate and less with wing morphology. Bat extinction risk is not randomly distributed phylogenetically: closely related species have more similar levels of threat than would be expected if extinction risk were random. Given the unbalanced nature of the evolutionary diversiﬁcation of bats, it is probable that the amount of phylogenetic diversity lost if currently threatened taxa disappear may be greater than in other clades with numerically more threatened species.

## **Biological Correlates of Extinction Risk in Bats**

**Kate E. Jones,[1,2,]**[*] **Andy Purvis,[1] and John L. Gittleman[2]**

1. Department of Biological Sciences, Imperial College at Silwood Park, Ascot, Berkshire SL5 7PY, United Kingdom;

2. Department of Biology, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia 22904-4328

_Submitted September 17, 2002; Accepted October 18, 2002; Electronically published March 28, 2003_

abstract: We investigated patterns and processes of extinction and threat in bats using a multivariate phylogenetic comparative approach. Of nearly 1,000 species worldwide, 239 are considered threatened by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) and 12 are extinct. Small geographic ranges and low wing aspect ratios are independently found to predict extinction risk in bats, which explains 48% of the total variance in IUCN assessments of threat. The pattern and correlates of extinction risk in the two bat suborders are significantly different. A higher proportion (4%) of megachiropteran species have gone extinct in the last 500 years than microchiropteran bats (0.3%), and a higher proportion is currently at risk of extinction (Megachiroptera: 34%; Microchiroptera: 22%). While correlates of microchiropteran extinction risk are the same as in the order as a whole, megachiropteran extinction is correlated more with reproductive rate and less with wing morphology. Bat extinction risk is not randomly distributed phylogenetically: closely related species have more similar levels of threat than would be expected if extinction risk were random. Given the unbalanced nature of the evolutionary diversification of bats, it is probable that the amount of phylogenetic diversity lost if currently threatened taxa disappear may be greater than in other clades with numerically more threatened species.

_Keywords:_ bats, extinction risk, independent contrasts, geographic range, predictive model, wing morphology.

_On-line enhancements:_ tab-delineated ASCII data

The most recent estimate of the current rate of mammalian extinction falls between 36 and 78 times the background rate measured over the past 65 million years (Regan et al.

2001). This and patterns of extinction in other taxa strongly suggest that the extent and rate at which species are currently being lost is comparable with the five mass extinctions of the geological past (May et al. 1995; Pimm et al. 1995; Hughes 1999; Jablonski 2001; Myers and Knoll 2001; Regan et al. 2001). Accumulating evidence supports the hypothesis that the risk of extinction is nonrandomly distributed among taxa (Bennett and Owens 1997, 2002; Russell et al. 1998; Mace and Balmford 2000; Purvis et al. 2000 _b_ , 2000 _c_ ; Bennett et al. 2001; see Purvis et al. 2000 _a_ for a review). Typically, extinction risk is clustered within closely related species, and as these share many of the same attributes, this suggests that certain traits may predispose species to extinction. Specializations, such as high trophic level, limited powers of dispersal, and small geographic ranges, are most often suggested as being linked to an increased extinction risk (McKinney 1997; Purvis et al. 2000 _a_ ). Additionally, the rate at which species adapt to biotic change may also affect their likelihood of extinction; for example, long generation times may decrease the rate at which they can adapt to change.

Understanding patterns of threat and species extinction is a major goal of conservation biology. Identification of those attributes that predispose species to extinction would help predict outcomes of different future scenarios and facilitate proactive conservation efforts, thereby helping to minimize human impact on biodiversity. However, going from an explanatory framework to a predictive model would require knowledge of which traits increase extinction risk across clades and how the importance of these as predictors alters with the particular set of causal processes influencing extinction (Owens and Bennett 2000). Within primates and carnivores, Purvis et al. (2000 _c_ ) found that a similar set of traits (small geographic range, high trophic level, low population density) predicts extinction risk in both orders, although importance of body size and life history differs significantly between orders. The generality of these results is unknown. The commonly nonrandom pattern of extinction is likely to be a multidimensional jigsaw puzzle: extinction-promoting traits may be clade, time, and location specific and may change with the nature of the threatening process (Purvis et al. 2000 _a_ ; Bennett et al. 2001). Finding the pieces of this

jigsaw puzzle to formulate generalities for the current extinction crisis will provide us with the means to advance from an explanatory framework to a predictive model. This study of extinction risk in bats aims to provide another piece of the jigsaw.

Bats are the second most species-rich order of mammals (925 extant and recently extinct species at a conservative estimate; Koopman 1993). They form a clade containing species of typically small body sizes but very diverse ecologies, life histories, and morphologies (Arita and Fenton 1997). Bats are important members of many communities, with pollinators and seed dispersers being keystone species and insectivores regulating nocturnal insect populations (Mickleburgh et al. 2002). The morphological, behavioral, and ecological correlates of bat extinction risk have never been examined comprehensively. Because of their unique adaptations (powered flight and many other distinctive morphological, sensory, and life-history adaptations; Jones and MacLarnon 2001), the extinction-promoting traits of bats are likely to differ from those in other mammal clades. Over 25% of bat species are classified as extinct or threatened (Mace and Balmford 2000): 12 species are recently extinct, 29 species are critically endangered, 37 species are endangered, and 173 species are vulnerable (Hilton-Taylor 2000). Although the proportion threatened is slightly lower than the overall mammalian threat frequency of 0.26 (Mace and Balmford 2000), a further 209 species are clasas near threatened.

We examined the pattern of extinction and threat within bats in a phylogenetic context and tested simultaneously a range of hypotheses relating extinction risk in bats to body size, life history, morphology, foraging ecology, and

biogeography. Additionally, we examined whether the same attributes are important in the two different major clades within the order: Megachiroptera and Microchiroptera. Extinction patterns may differ between these two suborders because there are substantial differences in their body size, ecology, and life history (Mickleburgh et al. 1992; Hutson et al. 2001), and studies have suggested that these two suborders are only distantly related (Megachiroptera more closely related to primates than to Microchiroptera; reviewed in Jones et al. 2002). We also determined whether the traits promoting extinction risk in bats are the same as those already identified as important in other clades such as primates and carnivores (Purvis et al. 2000 _c_ ) and birds (Gaston and Blackburn 1995; Bennett and Owens 1997; Owens and Bennett 2000).

## **Methods**

Data were assembled from the literature, building on the database compiled by Jones (1998). Variables were chosen to allow tests of the same hypotheses as previous analyses of extinction correlates in carnivores and primates (Purvis et al. 2000 _c_ ) and birds (Bennett and Owens 1997). Specifically, we collected the following characteristics (see table 1 for sample sizes): extinction risk, current geographic range, island status, adult body mass, reproductive rate, and group size. Extinction risk (from Mickleburgh et al. 1992; Hilton-Taylor 2000; Hutson et al. 2001) was recoded (following Purvis et al. 2000 _c_ ) as least concern p 0, nearthreatened p 1, vulnerable p 2, endangered p 3, critically endangered p 4, extinct p 5 (data-deficient species [37] were excluded). Current geographic ranges (km[2] )

were obtained from the most recent available published species range maps by digitizing the area into a Geographic Information System (ArcView 3.2). Where no range maps were available, the minimum area convex polygon (MACP) of published point data was calculated excluding areas of water. Where point location data were too few to calculate an MACP (!3 points), we assumed that the species occupied a set area of 1,000 km[2] for each recorded locality for mainland species or the entire area of the island for island populations, whichever was smaller. Island status was coded nonendemic p 0 and endemic p 1. Adult body mass was measured in grams. Rate of reproduction is correlated in mammals (independent of body size) with many life-history parameters (Read and Harvey 1989), and here we used the following life-history traits as surrogate measures of it: gestation length (days, excluding any period of delay), litter size, age at sexual maturity (months), and numbers of litters per year (one litter per year p 0, more than one p 1). Group size was measured as maximum roost size.

Further variables without parallel in other mammalian orders were also collected to test hypotheses specific to bats. Wing morphology has been shown to be an important predictor of many traits, for example, ecological foraging niche, community structuring, dispersal abilities, behavior, and home range area (Norberg and Rayner 1987; Norberg 1990; Findley 1993; Jones et al. 1995; Arita and Fenton 1997; Entwistle et al. 2000). These traits have been shown to influence extinction risk in other taxa. We therefore collected data on the two most important measures of wing morphology: aspect ratio (wingspan squared divided by wing area, or the ratio of wingspan and mean wing width) and wing loading (Nm[][2] [body mass times gravity acceleration] divided by wing area). The aspect ratio describes the shape of the wings: a high aspect ratio corresponds with long narrow wings and energy-efficient flight, and a low aspect ratio corresponds with short, broad wings and less efficient flight. Wing loading, a measure of the surface area of the wings compared to the weight of the body, is positively correlated with minimum speed required for flight and negatively correlated with maneuverability. Bats with low wing loadings are able to fly more slowly and turn more tightly and quickly than bats with high wing loadings (Norberg and Rayner 1987). The most recent and comprehensive bat taxonomic authority (Koopman 1993) was used to define the species considered. Koopman (1993) is also the only comprehensive taxonomic source that traces bat species name changes (synonyms). Tracing synonyms is crucial in order to gather comparable trait and phylogenetic data for each species from the primary literature and to calculate species trait values for each variable. In our analysis we transformed all the original species names given in each data source

into their currently recognized names, and then, for each species, we averaged data for each variable from different subspecies or geographic localities with the following exceptions: geographic range (where subspecies ranges were added together), litters per year and maximum roost size (where the maximum value was taken from the range available), and island status (where the minimum value of island status, i.e., “not endemic to islands,” was taken). Obtaining International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) threat data for each species was complicated by the fact that the available sources (Mickleburgh et al. 1992; Hilton-Taylor 2000; Hutson et al. 2001) do not strictly use Koopman’s (1993) taxonomy and recognize many more species but do not provide details of species synonymies.

In our analysis we calculate IUCN threat for each species as the lowest category of threat assigned to any of its subspecies or synonyms. Species that they recognize but that are not found in Koopman (1993; i.e., those described after its publication) are not considered here. This led to a discrepancy between the numbers of threatened and extinct taxa reported here and those of the IUCN (223 threatened and nine extinct vs. 239 threatened and 12 extinct for this analysis and IUCN, respectively). Size measurements are the average of both males and nonpregnant females. Sexual dimorphism is unlikely to bias the size calculation, as dimorphism is rare in bats. For example, from our data set, the average ratio of female to male mass for each species (for which we had both male and female mass) was 1.02 (SD p 0.17, _n_ p 344), with 0.93 and 1.11 the first and third quartiles of the distribution, respectively. Litter size is less variable in bats than other mammals: in the majority of species, adults have only one infant (56 out of the 328 species in our data set have a mean litter size of 11). Although the lack of variation in litter size may affect its explanatory power in our models, including litter size in the suite of tested variables enables comparison with previous studies on other mammals and birds (particularly) that do use this metric. Data and source details are available as downloadable files in the electronic edition of the _American Naturalist_ and from the corresponding author on request.

The distribution of threat in bats was examined by comparing the observed proportion of threatened and extinct species in suborders and families to the proportion for the order (using the bat threat frequency of 0.24 and the bat extinction frequency of 0.01; table 2), following methods developed for birds (Bennett and Owens 1997). Significance of deviations of clades that were more threatened than average was tested using a one-tailed test against a null distribution generated from randomizations of the data. Trait correlates of threat were examined using single or multiple least squares regression through the origin (Garland et al. 1992) on phylogenetically independent contrasts (Felsenstein 1985). Contrasts were generated using the CRUNCH algorithm of Comparative Analysis by Independent Contrasts (CAIC) computer package (Purvis and Rambaut 1995) using algorithms in Felsenstein (1985) and Pagel (1992). We used a species-level supertree of bats (Jones et al. 2002), which also follows the taxonomy of Koopman (1993), to calculate the independent contrasts. Both the equally weighted and differentially weighted versions of the supertree topology were used to generate contrasts, and as the results were not qualitatively different, we only present the analyses from the equally weighted topology. We found that using equal branch lengths best met the assumptions of CAIC (Purvis and Rambaut 1995), and this branch length transformation was used to stan-

dardize the independent contrasts for subsequent analyses. However, for several of the analyses this transformation failed to standardize the contrasts adequately (for details of diagnostic tests, see Garland et al. 1992).

The problem of incorrect branch length standardization has been tackled in several simulation studies (Martins and Garland 1991; Purvis et al. 1994; Diaz-Uriarte and Garland 1996). All found that the use of incorrect branch lengths increased Type I error rates to above nominal levels. Of particular relevance here, the two studies that used equal branch lengths to analyze data that evolved according to a gradual model (the worst-case scenario pertaining to the current analyses) gave Type I error rates of 8% (Martins and Garland 1991) and 12% (Purvis et al. 1994). However, Type I error rates of the same data using nonphylogenetic analysis were much higher: 16% and 31% (Martin and Garland 1991 and Purvis et al. 1994, respectively). Inspection of simulated data sets that produced Type I errors in the Purvis et al. (1994) study showed that there were typically a very small number of highly influential observations given undue influence by incorrect standardization. These observations were contrasts between sister taxa that were more distantly related than was being assumed, which suggests that the considerable differences between them were not being scaled down sufficiently to give homoscedasticity. A second cause of heteroscedasticity is data sampling error. Independent contrasts methods assume that differences among species have evolved rather than having arisen through a combination of evolution and imprecise measurement of species mean values. Closely related species may appear very different in a comparative data set, with most of the difference arising through sampling error. This difference is assumed to have evolved in a short time, so the scaled contrast has undue influence (Purvis and Webster 1999).

These two sources of heteroscedasticity make different predictions about which contrasts have undue influence. The first source predicts that the contrasts will be among deeply divergent sister taxa while the second predicts that they will be among close relatives (within genera). In the latter case, it is reasonable to exclude the contrasts having undue influence because the difference represents mostly error. In the former case, such exclusion is harder to justify. We have inspected the contrasts having undue influence in our regression analyses (recognized by having a studentized deleted residual greater than 3) and have excluded them if they are within-genus contrasts (on the grounds that such contrasts reflect mostly noise) but not if they are at higher taxonomic levels (on the grounds that they may reflect signal). These are the regressions we now report; we also note whether the significance was affected by inclusion of such points or by exclusion of all influential observations (as done by Jones and Purvis [1997]).

Because of intercorrelations among predictors, we also used multiple regression with model simplification to find minimum adequate models (MAMs; Crawley 1993) for extinction risk across the order and within each suborder (see methodology in Purvis et al. 2000 _c_ ). We included all variables in the MAMs that were found to be significant in predicting risk in the single or multiple regression analyses. Additionally, body size was included in the MAMs (although not a significant predictor of extinction risk) because of its additional intercorrelations with wing morphology and life-history variables (Norberg and Rayner 1987; Jones and MacLarnon 2001). The importance of collinearity in all multiple regression analyses was investigated, and in no case was variance inflation greater than 3 (Petraitis et al. 1996).

Although for the majority of bat species, extinction risk has been assigned with little regard to life history, morphology, or ecology (A. Hutson, personal communication), we recognize the potential for circularity in these analyses. Therefore, we first carried out analyses on all assessed species (873 species) and then excluded those species from the analysis whose assessment criteria may have had a life-history basis (10 species; IUCN criteria A1–2 [d–e], B3 [a–d] and E; Hilton-Taylor 2000). As a further analysis, we selected only those species whose threat status was assigned solely on the basis of past declining populations (23 species, IUCN criteria A1 [a–c]; Hilton-Taylor 2000) and compared their traits to nonthreatened species (least concern) using the BRUNCH algorithm of CAIC (Purvis and Rambaut 1995). BRUNCH selects nonnested, nonoverlapping sets of taxa across the phylogeny and calculates an independent contrast where there has been a change in extinction risk (see Purvis and Rambaut 1995, p. 249, for a full specification of the BRUNCH algorithm). All the contrasts in the independent variable (i.e., extinction risk) are set to positive, so if the evolution of the traits under investigation are uncorrelated, then roughly half the contrasts in the dependent variable (e.g., body size) will be positive and the other negative, with a mean not significantly different from 0 (Purvis and Rambaut 1995). Significance was tested using a Wilcoxon sign rank test on the generated contrasts. All continuous variables were loge transformed, and all statistical tests were twotailed (except for threat proportions) and were performed using SPSS/PC, release 10.0 (Norusis 1993).

## **Results**

## _Distribution of Extinction Risk_

Extinction risk and species-level extinctions are nonrandomly distributed between bat suborders and among families (table 2). Megachiroptera (family Pteropodidae) has

a significantly higher proportion of both threatened (34%) and recently extinct species (4%) than expected under a random distribution. Among Microchiroptera, extinction risk (22%) and extinction (0.3%) are also nonrandomly distributed. Strikingly, the monotypic higher-level clades (or those with two or three species) have a high proportion of threatened species, although this may be due to small sample sizes. Mystacinidae (New Zealand short-tailed bats) has a significantly higher proportion of species that have gone extinct than would be predicted from random. Extinction risk is highly correlated with evolutionary history (fig. 1). Species within the same genera, genera within the same family, and families within the same suborder have significantly more similar levels of threat using the spatial autocorrelation statistic Moran’s _I_ . Additionally, this analysis also illustrates the difference between the patterns of threat in Megachiroptera and Microchiroptera: levels of threat are significantly different between suborders (fig. 1; Moran’s _I_ p 0.17, _Z_ p 17.1, _P_ K .05).

## _Correlates of Extinction Risk_

Correlates of extinction risk using those species classified using noncircular IUCN criteria are shown in table 1. When predictors are tested singly, extinction threat in bats is significantly associated with small geographic ranges (the most important single predictor), island endemicity, smaller numbers of litters per year, and low wing aspect

The minimum adequate model (MAM; table 3) supports the suggestion that small geographic range sizes (partial correlation [pc] p 0.68) and lower aspect ratios (pc p 0.22) are independent predictors of extinction risk, which explains between them 48.3% of the total variance. There was some evidence to suggest that island endemicity was also an important independent predictor in the MAM ( _P_ p .06), although it was not significant in the multiple models. The results do not differ qualitatively when all species are included (i.e., including species whose threat ratings may be circular). Additionally, a single-predictor BRUNCH analysis using only the 23 species classified as declining compared to their closest nonthreatened sister taxa (lower risk : least concern; Hilton-Taylor 2000) supported an association between greater extinction risk and smaller geographic range sizes, island endemicity and lower aspect ratios (geographic range: number of contrasts p 16 [2 positive]/[14 negative]/[0 ties], _Z_ p 3.10, _P_ ! .01; island endemicity: _n_ c p 17 [8/0/9], _Z_ p 2.52, _P_ ! .05; aspect ratio: _n_ c p 7 [1/6/0], _Z_ p 2.20, _P_ ! .05). Predictors of extinction risk in Megachiroptera and Microchiroptera show different patterns; although small geographic range sizes and island endemicity were significant for both clades as single predictors, there were no other common predictors of extinction risk (table 1). As single predictors, low wing aspect ratios were an additional significant predictor of extinction risk in Microchiroptera, and this variable remained significant, controlling for geographic range and body mass. There was some evidence to suggest that island endemicity and group size were also

important in the multiple regressions, but the significance of these predictors depended on the inclusion of influential contrasts. For example, island endemicity lost significance when all the influential contrasts were included, whereas group size gained significance when all influential contrasts were deleted. Smaller numbers of litters per year and increased group size were correlated with increased extinction threat in Megachiroptera (table 1), although group size was not significant when all influential contrasts were included.

While the microchiropteran MAM is qualitatively the same as for the whole order, the megachiropteran MAM is different (table 3). Small geographic ranges (pc p 0.43) and lower numbers of litters per year (pc p 0.55) explain 51.5% of the variance in megachiropteran extinction risk with no significant role for aspect ratio; the correlation with litters per year is likely to be independent of variation in aspect ratio because these two variables are not significantly correlated ( _t_ p 0.07, _n_ s p 149, _n_ c p 100, _P_ p .94). A greater amount of variance in extinction risk was explained in the microchiropteran MAM (54.5%), and in addition there was some evidence that larger body sizes ( _P_ p .07) and larger group sizes ( _P_ p .07) were also independent predictors of risk in this suborder. To test the significance of the differences in the two suborders, we built a MAM starting with only those variables significant in at least one suborder, with suborder coded as a main effect and variable # suborder interactions. The resulting MAM (table 4) showed that neither the effect of aspect ratio nor the numbers of litters per year differed significantly between suborders. ## **Discussion**

## _Extinction Correlates_

We find that small geographic range sizes and low wing aspect ratios are significant independent predictors of extinction risk in bats despite there being potentially several different processes driving current extinction (Diamond 1984; Mickleburgh et al. 1992, 2002; Hutson et al. 2001). Habitat loss and fragmentation are probably the greatest threats to current biodiversity (Hilton-Taylor 2000), and under this process, both of these traits in bats would be expected to influence their extinction likelihood. Smaller geographic ranges may act through reducing the likelihood of population persistence in the face of problems caused by demographic stochasticity, local catastrophes, and inbreeding (Purvis et al. 2000 _c_ ). Geographic range size has been found to be an extremely important predictor of local abundance declines, extinction risk, and extinction in many different clades over a range of scales and time frames (e.g., Pimm et al. 1988; Gaston and Blackburn 1996; Davies et al. 2000; Purvis et al. 2000 _c_ ; Jablonski 2001), and its influence is further supported from the evidence presented here (see table 5). These analyses suggest that clades may be lost not because they are poorly adapted to predisturbance or postdisturbance selection pressures but because small geographic ranges limit their potential for

surviving an extinction crisis (Purvis et al. 2000 _a_ ; Jablonski 2001).

The association between extinction risk and geographic range found here may not be surprising given that some of the criteria used to assess species’ threat is based on their extent of occurrence or small population size (IUCN criteria B, C, and D): 95 out of the 239 threatened bats are classified using these criteria alone (Hilton-Taylor 2000). However, the relationship between increased risk and small geographic ranges still holds using those species whose assessment was assigned on the basis of only declines in populations (A1) with a similar slope coefficient to that obtained when all species are considered (declining species _b_ p 0.22, all species _b_ p 0.26). As would be expected, given that geographic range is the most important predictor of extinction risk, Megachiroptera on average have smaller geographic ranges than Microchiroptera (megachiropteran mean geographic range p 1.2 # 10 6 km[2] , SD p 2.9 # 10 6, _n_ p 158; Megachiroptera mean p 6.2 # 10 6 km2, SD p 6.8 # 10 6, _n_ p 309). Interestingly, the slopes describing the relationship between extinction risk and geographic range are not significantly different in the mammalian clades thus far studied (fig. 2, independent contrast slope _b_ p 0.343, _t_ p  26.51, _n_ s p 876, _n_ c p 582, _P_ ! .001 for primates, carnivores and Megachiroptera and Microchiroptera using data and phylogenies from this study and Purvis et al. 2000 _c_ , ANCOVA _F_ p 1.10, df p 3, 579, _P_ p .35). We find evidence to suggest that one feature of wing morphology (aspect ratio) is a significant predictor of extinction risk. Variation in wing morphology has been linked to many habitat, ecological, and foraging specializations as well as community structuring, dispersal, and behavioral traits in both bats and birds (Aldridge and Rautenbach 1987; Norberg and Rayner 1987; Norberg 1990, 1995; Findley 1993; McKenzie et al. 1995; Rhodes 1995; Keast 1996; Norberg et al. 2000). For example, lower aspect ratio wings have lower flight efficiencies and higher flight costs (Norberg and Rayner 1987) and are associated with species that have smaller foraging ranges and are poorer dispersers and migrators (Norberg and Rayner 1987; Jones et al. 1995; Arita et al. 1997; Lockwood et al. 1998; Entwistle et al. 2000). Wing shape is probably the result of multiple adaptive forces and is a compromise between conflicting aerodynamic requirements and ecologies (Norberg and Rayner 1987; Norberg 1990). It seems probable, then, that wing aspect ratio is perhaps a surrogate measure of other ecological variables that are the focus of extinction

processes: extinction risk is not a direct consequence of a particular wing design but actually directly correlated with other traits. For example, species with low-aspect-ratio wings (megadermatids, hipposiderids, rhinolophids, and phyllostomids) generally are more associated with foraging in cluttered habitats than are species with higher aspect ratios (molossids, noctilionids, emballonurids, and mormoopids). If these habitats are facing particularly severe threats, then wing designs adapted to them will also be associated with high risk of species extinction. Species with low aspect ratio wings also have smaller foraging ranges and low intercolony exchange of individuals (Jones et al. 1995; Entwistle et al. 2000). For example, species such as _Lasiurus cinereus_ and _Tadarida midas_ have high aspect ratio wings and foraging radii of over 6 km while species such as _Plecotus auritus_ , _Myotis emarginatus_ , and _Nycteris grandis_ have low aspect ratio wings and foraging radii of under 2 km (Jones et al. 1995). Such characteristics may provide a direct mechanism by which extinction processes can act. Smaller foraging ranges are likely to increase metapopulation extinction probabilities by reducing recolonization of empty patches. Smaller colony sizes are characteristic

of species with low aspect ratios (in 13 species of British bats [Entwistle et al. 2000] and in 89 species worldwide [this study]; 61 contrasts, _b_ p 0.01, _r_ 2 p 0.08, _t_ p 2.35, _P_ p .02). Colony size itself might be the focus of selection rather than any direct influence of wing design.

Evidence suggests that wing aspect ratio is not just an important predictor of extinction risk at the global scale (as found here) but also that its variation may indirectly explain local declines in both bats and birds. For example, species with low aspect ratio wing designs were more affected after habitat fragmentation in tropical forests (Australian insectivorous bats, Law et al. 1999; Philippine birds of prey, Gamauf et al. 1998). There is also some evidence that wing aspect ratios may indirectly affect local population declines after extreme environmental disturbance, for example, declines in abundances of five microchiropteran species in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Georges (see table 5; Jones et al. 2001). Although wing aspect ratio does seem to be an important predictor of bat extinction risk, the relationship within Megachiroptera and Microchiroptera is not clear. Wing aspect ratio variation did not predict extinction risk in Megachiroptera. Whether this is due to a lack of variation in aspect ratio within Megachiroptera (mean p 6.6, range p 5.6  8.7, _n_ p 36) versus the Microchiroptera (mean p 6.8, range p 4.8  14.3, _n_ p 224) needs to be confirmed with a more comprehensive database. A lack of variation in aspect ratio in Megachiroptera may reflect similarities of diet and foraging strategies within this family (Norberg and Rayner 1987). Interestingly, wing loading (the other commonly measured wing morphometric) did not seem to have any influence on extinction risk in bats. Although this variable may be important in determining habitat use (Norberg and Rayner 1987), wingloading has not been found to correlate with other biological traits in bats and so is perhaps not such a good surrogate metric for predicting extinction risk.

## _Outliers from the Model_

Following Purvis et al. (2000 _c_ ), we examined the outliers from our models by calculating the difference between predicted levels of threat (standardized to have the same mean and standard deviation as the observed threat values) from each suborder MAM to the observed IUCN threat level. Species that had a predicted level of threat that was greater than 1 threat category to that observed are shown in table 6. The majority of the species for whom our models underestimate threat are subjected to extrinsic, anthropogenic factors that our biological model currently does not include. Human activities that affect these (mainly cave or mine dwelling) species are hunting for food (e.g., the Megachiropterans _Pteropus mariannus_ and _Aproteles bulmerae_ ), roost disturbance through leisure ac-

tivities, development, deliberate persecution (e.g., _Myotis sodalis_ , _Myotis grisescens_ , _Plecotus townsendii_ , _Leptonycteris curasoae_ , _Macroderma gigas_ , _Rhinolophus hipposideros_ , _Rhinolophus euryale_ ), or prey poisoning (e.g., _Miniopterus schreibersi_ , _Tadarida brasiliensis_ ; Mickleburgh et al. 1992; Hilton-Taylor 2000; Hutson et al. 2001). Many of these species are also distributed unevenly with few, extremely large colonies of individuals (e.g., _M. schreibersi_ , _T. brasiliensis_ ), which makes their populations more vulnerable to human disturbance.

Our model also predicts a much higher level of threat than that currently observed in several species (table 6). Most of these species are island endemics or have otherwise restricted distributions (e.g., _Pteropus seychellensis_ , _Pteropus melanotus_ , _Brachyphylla cavernarum_ , _Erophylla sezekorni_ , _Monophyllus redmani_ ). Given the unknown population status of many bat species, our model suggests that the threat assignment of these species may need to be reconsidered.

## _Comparisons with Other Clades_

Many of the variables that have been found previously as predictors of extinction risk in other clades were not significant in these analyses (table 5). Our result is supported by a study of rarity in 150 species of neotropical bats in which no relationship was found between relative population density with body size (Arita 1993). It is suggested that flight might constrain the range of possible body sizes that are viable for powered flight (Norberg 1990), and this lack of variability may explain the unimportance of body size as a predictor of extinction. However, this is unlikely, as significant relationships between extinction risk and size have been found in birds (see table 5), although this may be because of the more threatened flightless species, which tend to be large. Other constraints specific to bats might be important in understanding the relationship between extinction risk and body size. For example, in echolocating bats (Microchiroptera), call parameters scale negatively with body size, and this might place constraints on maximum body size of species using certain foraging techniques (Arita and Fenton 1997; Jones 1999).

We find only limited evidence that life-history variation in reproductive rate is an important predictor of extinction risk in bats. This is in contrast to previous analyses in other mammalian clades and birds (table 5). Again, we do not think that this is solely a consequence of flight, as significant relationships between extinction and life histories have been found in birds (although these analyses controlled for fewer intercorrelated variables; table 5). The lack of a significant relationship with life history may be due to a Type II error produced through a lack of variability in the life-history data in bats and/or a confounding

There is some evidence that slower life histories (lower litters per year and earlier maturation ages) are associated with higher latitudes (Kunz and Stern 1995; Jones 1998; reviewed in Racey and Entwistle 2000). Further data are required to tease these factors apart. We did find that slow reproductive rates were a significant predictor of extinction in Megachiroptera (in line with other clades;

table 5); these species are restricted to a narrow latitudinal range and show the greatest variation in the numbers of litters per year of any clade of bats (Jones 1998). Further detailed studies are required to investigate the importance of geographic range and wing morphology as important extinction risk predictors in birds, as our results in bats would predict that they are.

## _Phylogenetic Pattern of Extinction_

Extinction risk in bats is phylogenetically nonrandomly distributed: levels of threat are more similar among species within the same genus, genera within families, and families within suborders. This phylogenetic nonrandomness in extinction risk is likely to underline a more general evolutionary process, as this is a common pattern in other clades, such as other mammals and birds (Bennett and Owens 1997, 2002; Purvis et al. 2000 _b_ ; Bennett et al. 2001; von Euler 2001). A nonrandom phylogenetic pattern in extinction risk causes greater than expected amounts of evolutionary history (in terms of phylogenetic diversity) to be lost when taxa do go extinct. This is because the extinction process will affect the whole clade where extinction risk is clumped (Purvis et al. 2000 _b_ ). The loss of phylogenetic diversity is predicted to be especially severe when the evolutionary history of the clade is unbalanced, that is, when there are many monotypic or species-rich clades and when the threat is particularly severe for species in depauperate or geographically restricted clades (Heard and Mooers 2000; von Euler 2001; Sechrest et al. 2002). Unfortunately, this may be the case here: the phylogeny of bats is extremely unbalanced (Jones et al. 2002). It seems probable, then, that the extinction of currently threatened taxa will cause a larger decline of phylogenetic diversity than in other more balanced clades (e.g., in carnivores; Bininda-Emonds et al. 1999). Bats as a whole are slightly less threatened than mammals generally (Mace and Balmford 2000; Yu and Dobson 2000) and have historically undergone rather fewer extinctions than would be predicted if mammal species had been extirpated at random (Alcover et al. 1998; Gittleman et al. 2001). However, the total amount of phylogenetic diversity lost if currently threatened bat taxa disappear may be greater than in other clades with numerically more threatened species (such as primates). It should be noted, however, that the record of historical extinctions may be subject to potential biases caused by differences in the distribution of sampling effort and the survival of evidence (see discussion in Gittleman et al. 2001). This may potentially bias our analyses of bat extinctions, although these biases are likely to be less marked for assessments of extinction risk.

There is much work to be done in explaining bats extinction risk: only 48% of the variance was explained by the variables considered, and further extrinsic anthropogenic factors need to be incorporated into the model. However, this analysis provides a quick metric for assessing extinction risk in bats that can be easily obtained from species accounts and morphometric measurements. In addition, extinction-promoting traits may change with the nature of the threatening process (see analysis in birds, Owens and Bennett 2000), and further analyses should

distinguish the effect of different processes (e.g., hunting vs. deforestation) on the power of our predictive models.
